comparison: Both address dating claims (C89-C102) but reach opposite conclusions. OpenEval finds the dating approach 'methodologically sound but indirect' and appropriately conservative (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers explicitly reject it as UNSUPPORTED, stating there is 'no direct or closely associated chronometric dating' and the chronological context is 'physically so far removed from these rock markings, as to be misleading at best.' This represents a fundamental disagreement on whether indirect dating via associated skeletal remains is acceptable.

Both address authorship attribution to H. naledi (C82-C88, C68-C69). OpenEval finds the exclusivity documentation and proximity of remains SUPPORTED though 'circumstantial.' Peer reviewers explicitly reject this as UNSUPPORTED and 'premature,' emphasizing that 'juxtaposition' does not demonstrate authorship and that 'this landscape has been home to multiple hominins.' Major disagreement on whether spatial association constitutes adequate evidence.

Both address tool evidence claims (C57-C61) with identical claim sets. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting 'direct evidence linking recovered materials to the engravings is lacking.' Peer reviewers also rate UNCERTAIN but are more critical, questioning the logical coherence: 'where are these objects?' and raising issues about lighting and tool transport. Both identify this as a significant evidentiary gap.

Both address methodological documentation (C130-C139) with identical claim sets. OpenEval finds methods SUPPORTED as 'appropriate for documentation' though preliminary. Peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED, criticizing the lack of 'image enhancements - which is standard in most rock art research' and noting that advanced imaging techniques used at sites like Blombos are 'not invasive or destructive' and should have been employed. Disagreement on methodological adequacy.

Both address whether markings are artificial vs. natural (C31-C47 overlap). OpenEval finds the systematic comparison against natural weathering SUPPORTED with 'well-documented' distinctions. Peer reviewers rate the broader artificiality question as UNCERTAIN, with all three stating the key question of 'artefactual or natural' is 'not definitively answered,' the argument is 'weak,' and 'the assertion that the rock engravings are anthropogenic remains unsupported by empirical evidence.' Major disagreement on sufficiency of evidence.

Both address detailed observations of marking characteristics (C19-C30 overlap). OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED with 'detailed observations' and 'observable superposition.' Peer reviewers include these claims in their broader UNCERTAIN evaluation about artificiality, questioning whether sufficient evidence exists to confirm the marks are intentional engravings rather than natural features.

Both address discovery documentation (C8-C15 overlap). OpenEval finds the documentation SUPPORTED with 'specific date, location, measurements' though notes interpretation as intentional requires additional evidence. Peer reviewers include these in their UNCERTAIN evaluation, questioning the fundamental claim that these are artificial markings at all.

Both address surface coating claims (C51-C56 overlap). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to undetermined material nature and speculative functions. Peer reviewers include these in their broader UNCERTAIN evaluation about artificiality. Both identify insufficient evidence, though peer reviewers focus more on the fundamental question of whether marks are artificial.

Both address relationship between engravings and geological features (C48-C50 overlap). OpenEval finds observations SUPPORTED though notes manufacturing difficulty inference is 'speculative but reasonable.' Peer reviewers include these in their UNCERTAIN evaluation about overall artificiality of the markings.

Both address exclusion of animal claw marks (C70-C81 overlap). OpenEval finds the systematic ruling out of alternatives SUPPORTED with 'sound logic.' Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, noting 'none of the reviewers challenge the exclusion of animal claw marks as an explanation.' This represents one of the few areas of agreement.

Both address Panels B and C (C62-C67) with identical claim sets. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED as preliminary observations with visual documentation. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, treating these as part of the broader uncertain evidence base without specific discussion. Both acknowledge these require further study.

Both address comparative archaeological context (C105-C123 overlap). OpenEval finds comparisons SUPPORTED with 'extensive comparative context' and 'valid' comparisons. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 1 stating 'I would draw little comfort from the similarities among equally unconvincing examples' and that weak arguments don't add up to a strong one. Disagreement on evidential value of comparisons.

Both address broader evolutionary context (C125-C129 overlap). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED with 'appropriate citations' and 'cautious' interpretation. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, acknowledging 'the shift in the academic climate' and accepting the broader evolutionary context even while questioning specific claims. Area of agreement on contextual framing.

Both address significance framing (C140-C143 overlap). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED as 'appropriate framing.' Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED for the broader context (C141-C143) while treating mortuary behavior (C140) separately. General agreement on the historical and theoretical framing.

Both address mortuary behavior claims (C140). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, noting they 'do not challenge the existence or dating of the mortuary behavior itself' which is 'treated as established context from previous publications.' Agreement on this established finding.

Both address geological and spatial context (C1-C7 overlap). OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED with 'well-documented geological and spatial context.' Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, noting 'none of the reviewers challenge the basic geological and archaeological context of the site.' This represents clear agreement on foundational contextual information.

Minor overlap on discovery location claims (C14-C15). OpenEval includes these in SUPPORTED discovery documentation. Peer reviewers include these in their SUPPORTED evaluation of basic site context. Agreement on factual site description.

Minor overlap on exclusivity claims (C68-C69). OpenEval includes these in SUPPORTED systematic ruling out of alternatives. Peer reviewers explicitly reject authorship attribution as UNSUPPORTED. The exclusivity of H. naledi presence vs. authorship attribution represents different aspects that lead to divergent conclusions.

Partial overlap on comparative context claims (C103-C104, C113-C114, C124). OpenEval rates comparative examples as SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers rate the broader evolutionary framing as SUPPORTED while questioning specific comparisons elsewhere. Mixed agreement depending on specific aspects of comparative analysis.
